name: The northern Renaissance's piety and public virtue
plain_explanation: Unlike the amoral, anarchic Italian Renaissance, the northern Renaissance combined enthusiasm for classical learning with genuine religious devotion and concern for public good, focusing especially on producing more accurate, scholarly texts of the Bible rather than on personal display of erudition.
precise_definition: Russell's characterization: the northern Renaissance 'was not anarchic or amoral; on the contrary, it was associated with piety and public virtue. It was much interested in applying standards of scholarship to the Bible... It was less brilliant and more solid than its Italian progenitor... more anxious to spread learning as widely as possible.'
why_it_mattered: Explains why Erasmus and More could combine deep classical learning with sincere Catholic piety and a reformist, rather than revolutionary, temperament -- and why they were poorly suited to the polarized world Luther's revolt created.
historical_origin: Emerged at the start of the sixteenth century in France, England, and Germany, before becoming entangled with the Reformation.
examples: Erasmus and Jerome's Greek New Testament (1516), used to correct inaccuracies in the Vulgate
competing_positions: The Italian Renaissance's amoral, anarchic character (Chapter II)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Shaped English public-school education (Greek and Latin grounding) 'almost exactly what he would have wished,' per Russell, into the modern era.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Deeply intertwined with ecclesiastical reform ambitions that stopped short of schism.
